lesson.title: Somewhere In Between: Average Speed Meets Instantaneous Speed
lesson.summary: The Mean Value Theorem is exactly why an average speeding ticket works: if your average speed over a stretch of highway exceeded the limit, there was a specific moment when your actual, instantaneous speed matched that average, whether or not any single radar gun caught it.
lesson.body:
Average rate of change over an interval and instantaneous rate of change at a single point are usually different numbers measuring different things: one summarizes an entire stretch, the other captures a single instant. The Mean Value Theorem is the precise statement connecting them: no matter how much the instantaneous rate wanders above and below the average during the interval, as long as the function is continuous and differentiable, there is guaranteed to be at least one instant where the instantaneous rate exactly equals the average rate for the whole trip.

This is the mathematics behind average speed cameras used on some highways, which measure the time a car takes to travel between two fixed points and compute average speed from distance divided by time, without ever directly measuring instantaneous speed at all. If that average speed exceeds the limit, the Mean Value Theorem guarantees there was some specific instant during the drive when the car's actual, instantaneous speed, the number a normal speedometer or radar gun would have shown, also exceeded the limit, even if no radar gun happened to be pointed at the car at that exact moment. The ticket is mathematically justified by an existence theorem, not by a direct instantaneous measurement.

Work through a concrete version. Suppose a car's position along a straight road is given by s(t) = t^2 + 2t, with s measured in miles and t in hours, and consider the interval from t = 1 to t = 4. Position is a polynomial in t, so s is continuous and differentiable everywhere, and the theorem applies on [1,4]. The average velocity over this interval is [s(4) - s(1)] / (4-1). Compute the endpoint values: s(4) = 4^2 + 2(4) = 16 + 8 = 24, and s(1) = 1^2 + 2(1) = 1 + 2 = 3. So average velocity is (24-3)/3 = 21/3 = 7 miles per hour. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees some instant t = c in the open interval (1,4) where the instantaneous velocity, s'(c), also equals 7. Since s'(t) = 2t + 2, set 2c + 2 = 7, giving 2c = 5, so c = 2.5, which does lie in (1,4). Checking directly, s'(2.5) = 2(2.5) + 2 = 5 + 2 = 7, confirming that at exactly t = 2.5 hours, two hours and thirty minutes into the trip, the car's instantaneous speed matched the 7 mph average for the whole three hour stretch.

This connects two ideas that are each meaningful on their own, average rate of change as a description of overall change and instantaneous rate of change as a description of change at a single moment, and shows they are never fully independent: over any continuous, differentiable stretch, the two are guaranteed to coincide somewhere. That guarantee, not a coincidence about any one specific function, is the real content of the Mean Value Theorem applied to motion.
